title: Capacity Converter
context: Grade 3, the last working topic of the metric measures chapter. An adult sees sums with zeros. What is being settled is that a litre is a thousand millilitres, so changing a big unit into a small one multiplies and changing back divides, and that two capacities in litres and millilitres are added with the millilitres first and a full thousand carried into the litres. A child who writes the litres and the millilitres side by side as one number will write 13 L 90 mL as 1390 mL, and will add the two columns as if they were the same unit.

writeup.why: Change litres into millilitres by multiplying by one thousand and millilitres into litres by dividing, change litres and millilitres together, judge a total, and add and subtract capacities in columns with a carry and a borrow, and find how many small cups fill a larger container.
writeup.look: A one litre jug that empties into millilitre drops at the left, a bucket with a litre scale and a millilitre scale beside it, a column board at the right with a litres column and a millilitres column, a row of small cups beside a larger container, and a drop count at the top left of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Capacity Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many millilitre drops have been counted so far. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The one litre jug stands at x 90, y 260, 160 wide and 320 tall, a recognisable flat glass jug with evenly spaced near-black marks and a label at every long mark. Tapping it tips it over a tray at x 90, y 600, 300 by 120, where a thousand drops land as ten small cups of 100 mL, each cup ten tens. The vermilion Unit fact ring sits between the jug and the bucket at x 300, y 380, 200 by 120, labelled Unit fact and Times 1000, with 1 L on its left and 1000 mL on its right. The bucket stands at x 540, y 240, 220 wide and 340 tall, drawn in its natural colours, with a litre scale down its left edge and a millilitre scale down its right edge, both starting at 0 at the bottom with evenly spaced near-black marks. A deep blue tag at x 540, y 600, 220 by 60 shows the amount given, a green tag beside it at x 780, y 600 the amount reached, and an amber tag at x 1020, y 600 a second amount or a carried or borrowed amount. The column board stands at x 800, y 240, 330 by 300, a board with a litres column and a millilitres column, the first amount on its top line and the second directly under it, and a carried or borrowed amount drawn above the column it joins. A row of small cups waits at x 540, y 640 beside a jar or a can at x 900, y 560 for the cup count. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing an amount in litres, in millilitres or in both into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The jug, the scales and the column board show the last working, with the given in a deep blue tag, the answer in a green tag and the carried amount in an amber tag.

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the first phase, when the jug is tapped, the thousand drops pour out in ten cups of a hundred, each cup tipping out ten tens, and the vermilion Unit fact ring pulses once for each cup, so the count climbs by a hundred every time. On the fourth phase, when the millilitres reach a full thousand, a whole litre lifts out of the millilitres column and slides over the top of the litres column to join it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a water tank stands beside the one litre jug with a deep blue tag holding a number of litres, and the vermilion Unit fact ring waits empty. On the second a bucket marked in millilitres stands with a deep blue tag holding a number of millilitres, and a row of empty litre jugs waits beside it. On the third a jar with a litre scale and a millilitre scale stands with a deep blue tag holding litres and millilitres together. On the fourth the column board is up with a litres column and a millilitres column, two amounts written under each other, and a row of small cups waits beside a jar. One thing moves, once: the jug, or the first column on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number of litres or millilitres, the jug emptied and filled, the bucket scales, and the column board with its carry and borrow. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on a drum, a pot, a tank, a bucket, a jug and a bottle, two buckets, a drum and a glass and a jar, each a real container.
voiceLines: A litre jug, a bucket with two scales, and a board with two columns. Let us change some amounts.
One litre is a thousand millilitres. What do all these litres make in millilitres?
A thousand millilitres fill one jug. How many jugs does this water fill?
Change the litres first. Then add the millilitres. Is the total right?
Start with the millilitres. Carry or borrow a litre if you need one.
A new amount. Which unit is bigger, and which way must the number go?
Free play. Empty the jug, read the scales and use the column board as you like.
Look at the jug. How many millilitres is one litre? Try the step again.
You changed litres and millilitres, and added and subtracted in columns.

source_tool.description: A one litre glass measuring jug stands at the left of the working area, 160 wide and 320 tall, drawn as a recognisable flat illustration with evenly spaced near-black marks. Tapping it empties the jug into a thousand millilitre drops, shown as ten small cups of 100 mL each, and each cup tips out ten tens of drops, so the thousand drops can be counted in tens, hundreds and then thousands. A vermilion ring labelled Unit fact and Times 1000 holds the step while this happens, with one litre on its left side and one thousand millilitres on its right side. Beside the jug stands a bucket drawn in its natural colours with a litre scale down its left edge and a millilitre scale down its right edge, both starting at 0. A deep blue tag shows the amount the question gives, a green tag the amount the child reaches, and an amber tag a second amount or a carried or borrowed amount. A column board stands at the right with a litres column and a millilitres column, the first amount on the top line and the second directly under it, and a carried or borrowed amount shown above the column it joins. A row of small cups waits beside a larger container, a jar or a can, for filling. A number pad types an amount in litres, in millilitres or in both, and the answer slot reads the typed amount back with its unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of millilitre drops that have been counted.
source_tool.art_direction: A kitchen shelf with jugs and buckets / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the jug. How many millilitres is one litre? Try the step again.
voice.onNext: A new amount. Which unit is bigger, and which way must the number go?
voice.opening: A litre jug, a bucket with two scales, and a board with two columns. Let us change some amounts.
voice.onFinish: You changed litres and millilitres, and added and subtracted in columns.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Empty the jug, read the scales and use the column board as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has poured a litre jug into a hundred millilitre cup ten times by hand and said how many millilitres are in a litre. The tool is what keeps the count of drops, what holds the times one thousand step in a vermilion ring while the jug empties, and what carries a full thousand into the litres column, which cups and a jug cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: One litre is one thousand millilitres. To change litres into millilitres, multiply by one thousand, and to change millilitres into litres, divide by one thousand. A capacity in litres and millilitres is changed by changing the litres first and adding the millilitres, so 13 L 470 mL means 13000 mL and then 470 mL more. To add two capacities, write a litres column and a millilitres column, add the millilitres first, and carry one litre when the millilitres reach one thousand. To subtract, take the millilitres first, and borrow one litre, which is one thousand millilitres, when the top millilitres are fewer. To find how many small cups fill a larger container, change both to the same unit and divide.
answer_key.wrong: The jug is emptied again and the drops are counted in tens, hundreds and thousands, and the column board shows the carried or borrowed amount moving between the two columns. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One litre is one thousand millilitres.
items.question: A water tank holds 19 L of water. How many millilitres is that?
items.checkpoint: To change litres into millilitres, multiply by one thousand.
items.misconception: Writing 190 mL or 1900 mL, with too few zeros, instead of multiplying by one thousand.

steps: One litre is one thousand millilitres.
items.question: A can holds 17000 mL of oil. How many litres is that?
items.checkpoint: To change millilitres into litres, divide by one thousand.
items.misconception: Multiplying by one thousand again, which makes the number bigger when the unit is bigger.

steps: Add the 470 mL: 13000 mL plus 470 mL is 13470 mL.
items.question: A jar holds 13 L 470 mL of juice. How many millilitres is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the litres into millilitres first, then add the millilitres.
items.misconception: Writing the litres and the millilitres side by side as 13470 L, or as 1347 mL.

steps: Write two columns: litres and millilitres.
120 mL is less than 460 mL, so borrow 1 L from the 6 L.
Subtract the millilitres: 1120 mL minus 460 mL is 660 mL.
Subtract the litres: 5 L minus 2 L is 3 L.
items.question: A bucket holds 6 L 120 mL of water. 2 L 460 mL is poured out into a can. How much water is left in the bucket?
items.checkpoint: When the top millilitres are fewer, borrow one litre, which is one thousand millilitres.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller millilitres from the larger, 460 mL minus 120 mL, instead of borrowing.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A drum holds 28 L of water. How many millilitres is that?
items.final_answer: 28000 mL, because one litre is one thousand millilitres and 28 times one thousand is 28000

items.question: A big pot holds 31000 mL of soup. How many litres is that?
items.final_answer: 31 L, because 31000 divided by one thousand is 31

items.question: A roof tank holds 34 L 380 mL of water. How many millilitres is that?
items.final_answer: 34380 mL, because 34 L is 34000 mL and 34000 mL plus 380 mL is 34380 mL

items.question: A jug holds 4 L 680 mL of juice and a bottle holds 2 L 530 mL of juice. How much juice is there in all?
items.final_answer: 7 L 210 mL, because 680 mL plus 530 mL is 1210 mL, which is 1 L 210 mL, and 4 L and 2 L and 1 L add up to 7 L

items.question: A bucket holds 37 L of water and a kettle holds 5 L. How many millilitres more does the bucket hold than the kettle?
items.final_answer: 32000 mL, because 37 L minus 5 L is 32 L and 32 L is 32000 mL

items.question: Two buckets each hold 13000 mL of water. How many litres do they hold together?
items.final_answer: 26 L, because 13000 mL and 13000 mL add up to 26000 mL and 26000 mL is 26 L

items.question: A child pours 29 L, 3 L, 140 mL and 140 mL of water into one drum and writes the total as 32140 mL. Is that right?
items.final_answer: No. 29 L and 3 L add up to 32 L, which is 32000 mL, and 140 mL and 140 mL add up to 280 mL, so the right total is 32280 mL

items.question: A glass holds 140 mL of juice. How many glasses fill a jar that holds 1 L 260 mL?
items.final_answer: 9 glasses, because 1 L 260 mL is 1260 mL and 140 mL nine times gives 1260 mL

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: tapping it empties it into a thousand millilitre drops, shown as cups of tens, with the Unit fact ring lit
a litre scale and a millilitre scale, each from 0, that read the same water in two units
holds a litres column and a millilitres column, with a carried or borrowed amount above the column it joins
tapping a small cup pours it into a larger jar or can and counts the cups
types an amount in litres, in millilitres or in both

teaching_notes: Pour a litre jug into a hundred millilitre cup ten times before the tool opens, and say how many millilitres are in a litre. Make the count of one thousand by tens: ten cups of a hundred millilitres, and each hundred is ten tens. To change litres into millilitres multiply by one thousand, and to change back divide by one thousand: ask which unit is bigger, and which way the number must go. For litres and millilitres together, say change the litres first, then add the millilitres, and never write the two numbers side by side as one number. In a column sum, start with the millilitres, carry a litre when they reach one thousand, and borrow a litre when the top millilitres are fewer. Use the true or false question to say why a total is right or wrong, and give the right one. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's sums, differences and conversions are the child's to try.
generation_prompt: Build a capacity converter tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A one litre glass measuring jug, 160 wide and 320 tall, stands at the left of the working area with evenly spaced near-black marks. Tapping it empties it into a thousand millilitre drops shown as ten small cups of 100 mL, each cup ten tens, while a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact and Times 1000 holds one litre on its left and one thousand millilitres on its right. Beside it a bucket has a litre scale down its left edge and a millilitre scale down its right edge, both starting at 0. A deep blue tag shows the amount given, a green tag the amount reached, and an amber tag a second or a carried or borrowed amount. A column board at the right has a litres column and a millilitres column, the first amount on the top line and the second directly under it, with a carried or borrowed amount above the column it joins. A row of small cups waits beside a larger jar or can, and tapping a cup pours it in and counts it. A number pad types an amount in litres, millilitres or both, and the answer slot reads it back with its unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of drops counted. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Tap the jug to empty it into drops. Change litres and millilitres into each other. Then add and subtract on the column board.
